examples.text: Melting solid tablea cacao in hot water is a physical change because no new substance is formed!
A sealed glass of ice water weighs exactly the same before and after the ice cubes melt completely into liquid water!
In a warm, dry spot, water evaporates faster! This means your beautiful crystals will form much more quickly.
In distillation, a mixture is boiled so one liquid evaporates, then the vapor is cooled back into a pure liquid!
Ice candy starts as liquid juice poured into a tube! Inside the freezer, the cold hardens it from a liquid into solid ice.
When you cool a liquid, its particles lose energy and slow down until they lock tightly together — that's freezing! It's how water becomes ice in your freezer.
Fog forms when air cools down and the water vapor inside it condenses into tiny droplets!
When warm moist air rises high up, it cools down! The invisible water vapor then condenses into tiny liquid droplets that form clouds.

Draw this flowchart for water: solid → liquid (melting); liquid → gas (evaporation); gas → liquid (condensation); liquid → solid (freezing). Add or remove heat to explain each arrow. Water remains the same substance through these changes.
Melting needs heat! That is why ice melts when its surroundings are warm.
The sun provides the heat energy that powers the whole water cycle by causing evaporation!
When sweat evaporates from our skin, it takes heat away from the body to cool us down!
Put dry ice in warm water, and it sublimates fast to make thick fog for cool stage effects!
Salt dissolving in water is a physical change, not a new substance! It is still salt, and you can get it back by evaporating the water.
Changes of state like melting, boiling, evaporating, or freezing are just physical changes because the substance stays exactly the same!
Oxidation is a chemical change because it creates a brand new substance that cannot easily be turned back!

Is rusting a chemical change?

Yes! It makes a new substance that can never turn back into the original iron.

Can melting and freezing be reversed?

Yes! Ice can become water, and water can become ice again.
When heated, solid coconut oil melts into a clear liquid — a reversible physical change you can see!

Melting ice and freezing water can reverse one another: the substance remains water. Rusting forms a new substance, so simply cooling the rust does not turn it back to iron. Physical changes keep a substance’s identity; chemical changes form new substances. Ease of undoing a change is a clue, not a rule: cutting paper is physical even when it is hard to undo.
Brass is a solid solution of copper and zinc, proving that solutions can exist in the solid state!
Stir brown sugar into cold calamansi juice, and watch it dissolve to form a uniform liquid solution!
Muddy water is an example of a suspension because the mud settles when the water stands still!
Beach sand in Boracay is a heterogeneous mixture! It's made of crushed coral, shells, and quartz minerals.
The shiny brass used in T'boli belts and ornaments is an alloy, which is a mixture of two metals: copper and zinc!
The exact amount of each metal mixed changes the alloy's properties, creating many different kinds of steel for different uses!
Almost all the air we breathe is just two gases! About 99% of it is nitrogen and oxygen.
Air is a mixture of gases! It is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, not just one pure substance.
Almost all the air we breathe is just two gases! About 99% of it is nitrogen and oxygen.
Air is a mixture of gases! It is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, not just one pure substance.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) is super tiny! It makes up only about 0.04% of the air we breathe.

What form does carbon take in the air?

In the air, carbon exists as a gas—it's called carbon dioxide, or CO2!
The invisible air around us is actually a gaseous mixture! It contains nitrogen, oxygen, and different amounts of water vapor.
Air holds hidden water vapor! When this invisible gas touches a cold glass, it turns into tiny water drops, making the glass wet.
In decanting, the heavy solid settles at the bottom. Then, the clear liquid is gently poured off!
In decantation, let the heavier solid settle at the bottom. Then, carefully pour off the clear liquid on top to separate them!
During winnowing, grain is tossed in a flat tray! The moving air blows away the light husks, while the heavier rice grains fall right back down.
A bilao is a flat woven tray for winnowing! Grain is tossed in the air so the breeze carries off light chaff while heavier grains fall back down.
Because oil floats, it's easier to gather when it spills! Workers use floating barriers to corral the oil in one place before scooping it all up.
Scooping is a separation technique where you use a scoop or spoon to remove an easily recognized substance from the rest of a mixture.
Picking is the simplest separation technique, where you use your hands or a tool to choose and remove substances from a mixture one by one.
We boil sweet cane juice until the water evaporates, leaving yummy sugar crystals behind!
In Philippine salt beds, seawater is left in the hot sun. It evaporates, leaving the yummy salt behind!
The particles in a suspension are large, so you can easily separate them by filtering!
A charcoal water filter uses porous carbon to remove impurities and odors from a liquid solution!
A sieve with smaller holes, or fine mesh, blocks much finer particles than a sieve with large holes!

How does sieving separate mixtures?

Fine bits fall through small holes, while bigger pieces stay on top!
Separating with a magnet is quick and clean because no water or pouring is needed!
You can use a magnet to easily separate tiny bits of iron from sand or any mixture!
Separating with a magnet is quick and clean because no water or pouring is needed!
After harvesting, rice is threshed to separate the grains from the stalks and straw.
Separating with a magnet is quick and clean because no water or pouring is needed!
After harvesting, rice is threshed to separate the grains from the stalks and straw.
The independent variable is the factor that is changed or manipulated in an experiment to see what will happen.
The independent variable is the factor that is changed or manipulated in an experiment to see what will happen.
The dependent variable is the one factor you measure in a fair test, because it shows the effect of the change you made.
Controlled variables are kept the same throughout an experiment so they do not influence the results.

To test whether stirring changes how quickly sugar dissolves, change only the stirring condition. Measure the time until no sugar crystals are visible. Keep the amount and type of sugar, water volume and temperature, and cup the same. Repeat each condition at least three times and record every result.
Three trials means doing the exact same test three times! It doesn't mean trying three different ideas just once each.
After three or more trials, scientists use the average! This keeps one odd measurement from pulling the final answer too far.
Accurate measuring means using the marks on your tool carefully! Never guess the last digit from far away.

How do you get an accurate reading from a thermometer?

Look at the thermometer at the exact same level as your eye!
A person has one heart, and it pumps blood all around the body.
Your heart beats slower when you are resting than when you are exercising.
Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to every part of your body.
Blood carries oxygen from your lungs to every single part of your body.

What do arteries do?

Arteries carry blood away from your heart and out to the rest of your body!
Inside your thin capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood right into your body's cells.

Draw and label a simplified circulation diagram: heart → lungs → heart → body → heart. The heart pumps; blood carries materials; blood vessels provide the routes. In the lungs, blood gains oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.
Many flowers release a sweet scent just to lure pollinators closer.
Flowers make sweet nectar as a reward, so pollinators visit and help spread their pollen.
Seeds come from a plant's flower and are often found inside its fruit.
Plant a jackfruit seed in the soil, and it can grow into a brand-new tree.
Kamote and cassava are usually grown from a piece of stem or cutting, not from seeds!
Malunggay is easy to grow — just stick a branch cutting into the soil, and it grows quickly!
Kamote and cassava are usually grown from a piece of stem or cutting, not from seeds!
Budding is done by making a T-shaped cut in the stem of a parent plant and inserting a mature bud called a scion under the bark.
In layering, a branch is bent down and covered with soil while still attached to the parent plant, and it grows roots right there.
In grafting, parts of two plants are joined to grow as one, like attaching a shoot of one tree onto another tree's trunk.

With your teacher, compare two propagation methods suitable for the same garden plant. Use at least three similar plants per method. Keep light, watering, soil, and observation time the same; record how many survive and grow. Cutting, budding, layering, and grafting suit different plants, so no method is best for every plant. An adult handles sharp tools.
Doing at least three trials, or replication, makes a fair test more reliable because similar results each time show the outcome was not just luck.
A chameleon is actually a reptile — a lizard with a backbone and scaly skin!
Animals with no backbone — like insects, worms, and shrimp — are all called invertebrates.
Animals with no backbone — like insects, worms, and shrimp — are all called invertebrates.
Earthworms have no bones at all, so they're called invertebrates: animals without a backbone.
A crab has no bones inside its body—instead, its hard outer shell supports it!
Many animals around us -- milkfish, the maya bird, dogs, carabaos, and frogs -- are all vertebrates because they have a backbone!

Why are plants called producers?

They make their own food—and they're the start of almost every food chain.
Water plants and algae cook up their own food using sunlight — that's why they're called the producers of the pond.
Animals are called consumers because they can't make their own food — they must eat other living things.

What eats the plant-eating animals?

Secondary consumers do — usually meat-eating carnivores, like a snake or a bird that eats mice.
Scavengers might seem gross, but they're vital -- they keep a healthy ecosystem clean and balanced.
Ants and beetles aren't just tiny bugs — they're scavengers too, cleaning up by eating dead animals.
The main decomposers in nature are fungi, like molds and mushrooms, and bacteria.
Decomposers get all their food and energy from breaking down dead plants and animals.
An omnivore eats both plants and other animals, making it a bridge that links two parts of the food web.
Decomposers close the loop of the food web, returning nutrients to the soil so producer plants can use them all over again.

Why do seeds spread far from the plant?

So they don't have to compete with their parent plant for water, light, and space to grow!
When food, water, or space is scarce, animals with the same needs compete for it — the stronger or faster ones are more likely to survive.
Ladybugs and lacewings are predator insects that hunt and eat pest insects.
Many predators hunt using sharp teeth and claws to catch and eat their prey.

Use a reliable science book or research summary to compare competition and predation. Competition involves organisms needing the same limited resource; predation involves a predator eating prey. Record the organisms, what the source says happens, and its title and author. A photograph of two animals together is not enough to prove either interaction.
An ecosystem is made of biotic parts, like plants and animals, and abiotic parts, like water, light, temperature, and soil.

What exactly is an ecosystem?

An ecosystem is all the living things — plants, animals, microbes — and nonliving things — water, air, soil, sunlight — in one place, all interacting so a change in one affects the rest.
Corals thrive in warm, shallow, and clear water where sunlight can reach all the way down.
Coral reefs need clean, shallow, warm water reached by sunlight in order to grow and thrive.

An ecosystem is made of biotic parts, like plants and animals, and abiotic parts, like water, light, temperature, and soil.
A shrimp is cold-blooded, so its body temperature depends on the temperature of the water it lives in.

What exactly is an ecosystem?

An ecosystem is all the living things — plants, animals, microbes — and nonliving things — water, air, soil, sunlight — in one place, all interacting so a change in one affects the rest.
The clownfish makes its home inside a sea anemone to stay protected from predators!
Constant cleaning on the reef helps keep the number of parasites on fish under control.
Earthworm tunnels make it easier for plant roots to grow down into the soil.
Tree roots hold soil firmly in place, helping prevent erosion and landslides!
A bolt and a twist-on jar lid are types of screw!
We use a screw to hold things tightly together, like pieces of wood!
A wedge is used to cut or split things, just like a knife, an axe, or scissors!

What simple machine helps you roll heavy things up easily?

A ramp is a type of inclined plane!
A longer, gentler ramp needs less force to use than a short, steep one!
It takes less force to push a heavy load up a ramp than to lift it straight up!

How does a woodpecker find its food?

A woodpecker’s sharp beak acts as a wedge, concentrating force to split tree bark and uncover hidden insects!

Why is a long, thin wedge better for splitting?

Because it multiplies your pushing force more, making it split or cut much easier than a thick one!
We use a lever to make work easier! It needs less effort to move a really heavy object.
A third-class lever always has a mechanical advantage of less than 1, multiplying distance instead of force!
A fixed pulley changes the direction of force! You can pull down to lift a load up.
A pulley doesn't create energy! It just makes your job easier by spreading out the force.
On a real ramp, you need a little extra force compared to a perfect one because friction resists the motion!

What is the trade-off when using a ramp?

A ramp lets you use less force, but you must move the load over a longer distance!
When the fulcrum sits between the load and your hand, pushing down makes the load go up! It changes the force's direction.
In a lever fair test, the distance you change is the independent variable. The force you measure is the dependent variable!
When the fulcrum sits between the load and your hand, pushing down makes the load go up! It changes the force's direction.
Testing direction change is fun! Watch the load move up when you push the lever down, and record this opposite motion in your notes.
In a lever fair test, the distance you change is the independent variable. The force you measure is the dependent variable!
Grab a meter stick! Measure the distance from the fulcrum to the load, and from the fulcrum to your hand.
A returning echo is quieter than the original sound because it spreads out and loses energy while traveling!
A wave carries energy through the water, but the water doesn't travel! It just moves up and down as the energy passes by.

Why does sound get fainter as it moves away?

Its energy spreads out over a wider space as the sound wave moves away from its source!
As waves travel farther from their source, their energy spreads over a wider area. That's why sound and light grow weaker the farther away you get from them!
Count how many crests pass a mark in ten seconds to compare frequency, a cool movement feature besides shape and size!
The first messy splash isn't the wave feature to describe; wait for the clean moving bands, then talk about crest, trough, and path!
The tank shows three cool features: shape like crests and troughs, size like width and height, and movement like travel, bending, and bounce!
The "width" of a wave in the tank is the spacing between the moving bands. This distance is the wavelength you observe!
The tank shows three cool features: shape like crests and troughs, size like width and height, and movement like travel, bending, and bounce!
When part of a wave front enters shallower water, it slows down and the whole front bends! You can easily see this change of direction in the tank.
Use a straight metal barrier in the tank to watch wave reflection! If you curve the barrier, the shape of the bounced pattern changes too.

Can reflected crests meet incoming ones?

Yes! They make a busy crisscross near a wall, so look carefully before naming just one travel direction.
When part of a wave front enters shallower water, it slows down and the whole front bends! You can easily see this change of direction in the tank.

Why level the tray before adding water?

A tilted tank makes one side shallow and secretly bends every wave you study!
Resonance happens when something is pushed at its natural frequency. The waves add up and grow in amplitude, like a guitar string or air inside a flute!
A shout travels way farther than a whisper! That's because a shout has larger amplitude — it carries more energy and stays strong over a bigger distance.
The frequency of sound is measured in Hertz (Hz), meaning the number of cycles per second!
The hertz measures frequency! It counts exactly how many times something repeats in just one second.
Wavelength is simply the exact distance from one wave's crest to the very next crest!
When a source or observer moves toward the other, the observed wavelength gets shorter. When they move apart, it gets longer!
The speed of sound in a medium equals frequency multiplied by wavelength. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, and vice versa!
When a wave moves from air to water, its frequency stays exactly the same! Only the speed and wavelength change, but the waves per second never change.

Use a reliable science textbook diagram to label a wave: amplitude is maximum displacement from rest; wavelength is crest-to-crest distance; frequency is cycles per second; speed is distance traveled per second. Write the source title beside your notes and compare its labels with your water-wave observations.
Both kinds have a wavelength! It is measured crest-to-crest for a transverse wave, or compression-to-compression for a longitudinal wave.
Transverse waves show crests and troughs! Longitudinal waves show compressions and rarefactions. They are two different pictures of a cycle.
Energy travels along the wave in both kinds, but only transverse waves have a shake that is perpendicular to that energy path!
Both kinds have a wavelength! It is measured crest-to-crest for a transverse wave, or compression-to-compression for a longitudinal wave.
Energy travels along the wave in both kinds, but only transverse waves have a shake that is perpendicular to that energy path!

With a teacher, move one end of a rope side to side: a transverse pulse travels along it. On a loosely stretched spring, push and release the end along its length: a longitudinal compression travels. A marker on the rope or spring moves about its resting place while energy travels along the model. Keep movements gentle and away from faces.
When you stretch a slinky to the same length on a smooth, flat floor, the wave travels in a straight, even path!

A marker on the rope or spring moves about its resting place while energy travels along the model. Keep movements gentle and away from faces.
When a wave travels along a rope tied to a fixed post, it bounces back upside down, showing reflection at a fixed end!

A light paper ball at the end of a stretched slinky moves when the wave arrives, showing the wave carried energy to it!
A drumhead mostly moves up and down like a transverse motion, but the boom you hear is a longitudinal wave traveling in air!

How do particles move in a longitudinal wave like sound?

They vibrate back and forth in the exact same direction the wave travels!
Shaking a long bamboo pole up and down sends a transverse pulse along it! It's a great yard example, just like a jump rope.
A drumhead mostly moves up and down like a transverse motion, but the boom you hear is a longitudinal wave traveling in air!
A buzzing toy swung in a circle on a string sounds higher when it comes toward your ear and lower when it swings away!
The faster a horn moves toward you, the more the sound waves bunch up, causing a greater rise in pitch than a slow horn!
A buzzing toy swung in a circle on a string sounds higher when it comes toward your ear and lower when it swings away!
You'll notice the big drop in pitch right as the moving source passes you! It switches from coming closer to going away.
Draw circles packed tightly on one side of a moving dot! This shows why a listener on that side hears a higher sound.

Molten rock under the ground is called magma, and when it comes out of a volcano it becomes lava!
When one plate sinks beneath another, it melts in Earth's heat and forms new magma that can feed a volcano!
Mayon Volcano in Albay is a classic stratovolcano formed by many layers of hardened lava and ash!
When one plate sinks beneath another, it melts in Earth's heat and forms new magma that can feed a volcano!
Pinatubo in Zambales is an active volcano! Many thought it was asleep, but it suddenly erupted in 1991, proving volcanoes can wake up!
Kanlaon is the highest peak in the Visayas and an active volcano on Negros Island! It often has phreatic eruptions (steam explosions) and is closely monitored by PHIVOLCS to keep locals safe.
Volcano hazard maps show areas that could be hit by ashfall, lava, or lahar — helping families know if their home is at risk!
Find the nearest volcano by checking PHIVOLCS maps or asking your local government — they keep records of nearby hazards!

Why compare Mayon and Pinatubo?

Comparing Mayon's many eruptions with Pinatubo's rare giant blast helps families see that nearby volcanoes can follow very different clocks!

Do Philippine volcanoes always erupt at the same time?

Nope! Some years, several show unrest close together, while other years stay quieter, making activity come in uneven clusters.

With your teacher, use PHIVOLCS records to list a Philippine volcano’s eruptions during the last 100 years. Note dates, recorded hazards, and community effects; compare with family accounts. Gaps between past eruptions are not a timetable for the next one. A century of records covers only a small part of a volcano’s life.
Mayon showed strong unrest in 2018 with lava and ash! This is just one more event in its long pattern of waking many times.
Talking with elders about past eruptions is super helpful! It helps families learn if their volcano wakes up often or only after a very long rest.

When a volcano erupts, it spews out hot lava, ash, rocks, and gas into the sky!
Lava flowing from a volcano is super hot, reaching about 1,000 to 1,200 degrees Celsius!
When a volcano erupts, it spews out hot lava, ash, rocks, and gas into the sky!
Here in the Philippines, soil near volcanoes is very fertile because of the ash from eruptions!
When a volcano erupts, it spews out hot lava, ash, rocks, and gas into the sky!
Taal Volcano emits sulfur dioxide, which is a colorless gas with a very pungent odor!
A pyroclastic flow is a super hot, super fast rush of ash and gas racing down a volcano — and it's extremely deadly!
During an eruption, a volcano releases ash, toxic gases, and fast-moving flows of hot rock and gas called pyroclastic flows!
PHIVOLCS volcano alert levels are a numbered scale! It tells communities how serious the unrest is and what they should prepare to do.

Can we rush home right after a loud volcanic blast?

Not yet! Wait until PHIVOLCS lowers the alert and officials say the roads and slopes are truly safe.
PHIVOLCS volcano alert levels are a numbered scale! It tells communities how serious the unrest is and what they should prepare to do.
Around active volcanoes there is a danger zone where living is not allowed. When the alert level rises, people must evacuate for safety!
During heavy ash or explosions, stay in your assigned shelter! Don't walk home across open ground, even if the first big boom already passed.
During Alert Level 5, never walk closer just to take photos! Interpreting the alert means treating the eruption as a real hazard, not as a fun show.

The wet season is important to farmers because it gives water to the rice fields!
Time for sunny days! The dry season in the Philippines runs roughly from November to May.
The wet season is important to farmers because it gives water to the rice fields!
In the Philippines, lanzones and rambutan are usually harvested during the rainy months of August to October.

Rainfall patterns vary across Philippine regions. PAGASA describes several climate types; some places have no distinct dry season. Before planning planting, outdoor games, or travel, check your area’s seasonal pattern and the current local forecast. The same month can bring different weather to different islands.

What causes day and night on Earth?

Earth rotates once in about 24 hours!
Earth loves to spin! One full rotation, which gives us one complete day and night, takes exactly 24 hours.

Use a lamp as the Sun and mark your location on a globe. Keep the lamp fixed and rotate the globe: your mark enters the lit half for day, then the unlit half for night. This models Earth’s rotation. Moving the globe around the lamp models revolution, a different motion.
Earth has seasons because it tilts on its axis as it orbits the Sun!
Eclipses don't happen every month because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted, so the shadows usually miss!
We see different constellations all year because Earth orbits the Sun! For example, Orion is easier to spot during the cooler months in the Philippines.

Why do we see different constellations each season?

As Earth orbits the Sun, the part of space we face at night changes, showing us different constellations!
A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun, blocking the Sun!

How does a solar eclipse happen?

It happens when the Moon blocks the sun and casts its shadow on Earth!

When can a lunar eclipse happen?

Only during a full moon! That's when the Sun and Moon are on opposite sides of Earth.
During a lunar eclipse, the Moon turns reddish! Earth's atmosphere filters out other colors and bends only red sunlight onto the Moon.
Using a flashlight as the Sun, a large ball as Earth, and a smaller ball as the Moon helps us see how eclipses form when they align.

Move a tilted globe around a fixed lamp while keeping its axis pointing in the same direction. This model shows how Earth’s tilt changes sunlight angle and day length during its orbit, causing seasons. Put star labels around the model: the night side faces different constellations during the year. The model is not to scale.
Use the two end stars of the Big Dipper as pointers to find Polaris, the North Star!
Ancient sailors used constellations as their guide for direction when sailing across the sea!
The ancient Tagalogs named the Orion constellation Balatik, using it to track the changing seasons in the Philippines!

How did ancient Filipinos know when to plant crops?

They looked at the Moroporo star cluster, now called the Pleiades, to determine planting seasons!
One interview is not the whole Philippines! Different islands named different star patterns, so gather more than one local account!
Want to learn sky knowledge? Ask an elder for permission first, then listen to how their community named stars or warned about eclipses!
Want to learn sky knowledge? Ask an elder for permission first, then listen to how their community named stars or warned about eclipses!
Star names and eclipse sayings were ways of teaching — so your investigation is about how knowledge was communicated, not just listing pretty sky pictures!

How did ancient Filipinos know when to plant crops?

They looked at the Moroporo star cluster, now called the Pleiades, to determine planting seasons!

How did old Filipino farmers know when to plant rice?

They looked at the Balatik constellation, part of Ursa Major, to know the perfect time to plant!
